Microdrama platform Story TV's parent EloElo raises $80 million in Series C funding
ADVERTISEMENT
Bengaluru-based EloElo Group, the company behind microdrama platform Story TV, has raised $80 million in a Series C funding round led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. The company will deploy the fresh capital towards expanding its original content slate, taking its microdrama business to international markets and strengthening its artificial intelligence platform, Dolphin AI.
MIT Investment Co. and existing investors, including Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners, among others, also participated in the round.
Founded in 2020 by former Flipkart executive Saurabh Pandey, EloElo operates Story TV, which has more than 5,000 microdramas across six languages. The platform launches a new drama every three hours, while users spend an average of 95 minutes on it daily.
The company also operates Master, a micro-learning platform, Dolphin AI, an agentic AI creative suite, and Voxy AI, an AI companion agent. Across its applications, EloElo has more than 40 million monthly active users.

With the latest fundraise, the company's total capital raised has reached $130 million. EloElo said it recorded multi-fold revenue growth over the past year and operates across content creation, distribution and AI-powered production.
Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO of EloElo Group , said “A billion people now reach for the phone before any other screen, and the entertainment built for them will be video first, in their own language, in episodes that fit their day. That is the business EloElo Group is building: an AI-powered entertainment ecosystem that brings the next billion viewers storytelling beyond just clips. Story TV shows us what India wants to watch, and Dolphin AI gives us the economics to make it, which is how we have scaled with solid unit economics. Consumer AI will change how content is created, distributed and consumed, and we intend to lead that shift from India. articles.title: Robot-by-the-Hour Startup Tutor Intelligence Raises $75M Series B
articles.snippet: Robot-by-the-Hour Startup Tutor Intelligence Raises $75M Series B Wowtale
articles.text:
AI has transformed the digital world, learning to converse and code from the internet’s vast record of text and images.
The physical world has no such record to train on. For robots to take over the lifting, moving and manipulation that keep factories and warehouses running, they need data from real work in real facilities.
Tutor Intelligence , a Watertown, Massachusetts robotics company that collects that data by putting robots to work, announced a $75 million Series B. The round brings its total capital raised to $117 million, following a $34 million Series A last December.
Tutor came out of MIT CSAIL and builds across the full stack: robots, foundation models and deployments. It places fleets of internet-connected robots in customer production sites, where remote operators the company calls “tutors” assist with tasks. Every completed task generates real-world experience data that trains Tutor’s own robot foundation model. Better models let the robots handle more work, which leads to more deployments. The company describes this as a network of intelligence in which each new deployment strengthens the entire fleet.
Its robots are called Sonny and Cassie. Tutor sells robot work the way businesses already buy labor: by the hour or by the pick. Customers make no upfront purchase and sign no long-term contract, and Tutor handles deployment, maintenance and regular software and model upgrades. The robots work in some of the largest U.S. manufacturing and logistics networks, handling goods such as breakfast cereals, snacks, candy, cosmetics, home goods and toys.
Josh Gruenstein is co-founder and CEO, alongside co-founder Alon Kosowsky-Sachs. Gruenstein says the models let robots do jobs they have never done before and make robots affordable on a new level, and that the company can hardly build robots fast enough to meet demand.
Andreessen Horowitz led the round. Union Square Ventures , which led the Series A, and Neo , which led the seed round, also participated. The company did not disclose its valuation or revenue.
The funds will support frontier robot foundation model training and the manufacturing and deployment of Sonny and Cassie. Tutor’s robots now work in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago, and the company is on track to have more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027, all built in and deployed from the United States. Nearly a third of organizations that received Tutor robots in the past 12 months were existing customers installing more of them.
Competitive landscape
Tutor competes with a growing field of physical AI companies. On the general-purpose robot model side, Physical Intelligence raised $600 million at a $5.6 billion valuation last November, Skild AI raised $1.4 billion in January, and Generalist AI raised a $400 million Series A at a $2 billion valuation in June, followed by another $200 million in August. These companies put the model itself at the center of their pitch.
Closer to logistics and manufacturing floors, Dexterity raised $95 million to develop physical AI, and Foundry Robotics raised a $100 million Series A last month for AI-run robotic assembly plants.
Tutor also trains its own foundation models, but treats them as one layer of a service. What sets it apart is the business model: supplying robot work by the hour or by the pick and feeding the resulting field data back into training.

Israeli Startup 42AI Emerges from Stealth With $62.5 Million Seed Round
The Tel Aviv company is developing an AI model to predict human behavior, initially targeting financial markets, where 10 brokerages are already using its technology
Mandi Kogosowski
|
03/11/2026
Sponsored
Illustration: Rafael Minguet Delgado via pexels.com
Israeli startup 42AI has emerged from stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding accumulated over three years from its founders and Infinity Group.
The company was founded by CEO Amit Gal-Or, CTO Ehud Ezra, and chairman Amir Gal-Or, who also founded Infinity Group. As reported by TechCrunch, 42AI is developing a "behavioral world model" designed to predict individual decisions by identifying underlying psychological tendencies rather than relying solely on past behavior.
Initially targeting financial markets, the system analyzes data including customer onboarding, transactions, support calls, and voice sentiment to predict how individual traders may respond to changing market conditions. Brokerages can use these forecasts to anticipate trading direction and volume and adjust hedging strategies.
According to TechCrunch, the company is working with 10 large brokerages and has reached seven-figure revenue. Gal-Or also claimed that one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. It also also explores applications in fraud prevention , cybersecurity , and gaming
42AI claims 98% accuracy in predicting trading activity, although this measures whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not whether individual trades are correctly forecast.

The company says its Series B round, announced last week, will help Casap advance its AI platform as it looks to move its focus beyond fraud and disputes to automate other financial services operations.
Shanthi Shanmugam , Casap’s co-founder and CEO, said in a news release that the company began with disputes because it was one of financial services biggest challenges, though its ambitions were further-reaching.
“We wanted to prove that AI could do more than make work more efficient,” Shanmugam said. “It could fundamentally change the outcomes for financial institutions. Today we’re cutting fraud losses in half while resolving disputes in days instead of months. Now our customers are asking us to bring that same transformation to the rest of their operations.”
Casap’s platform includes specialized AI agents that investigate, make decisions and take action across financial institutions’ systems. The agents work across existing systems and apply the institution’s own policies and procedures, bringing in human workers in scenarios where their judgment is required.

The offering covers areas including fraud, collections, claims and “complex exceptions,” areas in which fragmented systems and manual investigations can cause financial loss, delays and lackluster consumer experiences, the release said.
“If all we get from the agentic era is the same outcomes happening faster, we’ve missed a huge opportunity,” Shanmugam said. “Our mission is to make outcomes that once seemed impossible the new standard for financial services.”
Meanwhile, recent research from PYMNTS Intelligence shows that companies employing multiple AI-powered fraud prevention tools are more likely to stop attempted theft before funds leave their accounts.
This offers “an encouraging direction for businesses strengthening payment defenses,” PYMNTS wrote Monday (Nov. 2), citing data from “Prevention First: Building a Smarter Defense Against Payments Fraud,” a report produced in collaboration with Bottomline .
The September report is based on findings from a July survey of 150 U.S. treasury and finance executives at companies with at least $100 million in yearly revenue.
“It finds that stronger fraud protection combines technology with reliable supplier verification and payment controls,” PYMNTS wrote. “AI can help identify suspicious activity, but companies still need to confirm who they’re paying. Think of those checks as several locks on the same door , each providing another opportunity to stop an intruder.”

articles.title: Humble Robotics Raises $51M Series A to Advance Autonomous Freight
articles.snippet: Humble Robotics Raises $51M Series A to Advance Autonomous Freight Unite.AI
articles.text:
Funding
Humble Robotics Raises $51M Series A to Advance Autonomous Freight
Published
November 5, 2026
Updated
November 6, 2026
By
Elara Nix, AI in Transportation & Autonomous Systems AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Humble Robotics announced a $51 million Series A on November 5, 2026, led by Obvious Ventures to fund customer pilots, testing and validation, early manufacturing and a broader family of autonomous electric freight vehicles. Existing investors Eclipse, Energy Impact Partners and others joined the round.
Humble also distributed the announcement through Business Wire. The new round follows a $24 million seed round announced on April 21, 2026, when the company emerged from stealth with the Humble Hauler. Eclipse led the seed, with Energy Impact Partners and others participating.
Humble said at the time that it completed its first prototype in just under six months. Founder and CEO Eyal Cohen previously worked on autonomous driving, electric vehicles and logistics at Apple, Uber and Waabi. The founding team also included people from Tesla, Waymo and Cruise.
A Cabless Vehicle and Operating Service
Humble calls its approach unified autonomy: the vehicle, driverless intelligence and operations are designed together for dock-to-dock movements among ports, rail terminals, warehouses and distribution centers. The Hauler combines the functions of a tractor, trailer and driver. Its operating model includes full-service freight transport with 24/7 remote operational support and charging, and the vehicle is designed to unload directly at a dock.
Target applications include port drayage, full-trailer shuttles between factories and distribution centers, container moves inside rail yards and short legs between carrier terminals. Humble also plans to plug into existing charging infrastructure wherever possible.
The cabless Class 8 platform’s standard configuration moves 40-foot international and 53-foot US containers. A universal lock-and-twist interface is intended to support multiple vehicle configurations, and the platform uses an all-electric eAxle powertrain. Humble’s technical specifications list a 200-mile range and 55 mph speed.
L4-capable sensor pods combine automotive cameras, lidar and radar for 360-degree coverage. Redundant automotive-grade controls also form part of the vehicle’s safety architecture.
Vision-First AI for Regional Routes
Humble says its starting market, regional freight routes under 250 miles, accounts for 87% of US truck tonnage. The initial operating plan centers on short, repeatable dock-to-dock runs.
The company contrasts that choice with long-haul highway driving, which can require an 80,000-pound driverless vehicle to operate at 65 mph in rain, snow and fog, and describes retrofitted diesel trucks as risky and expensive for that task.
The Humble Driver uses a vision-first, end-to-end foundation model alongside safety constraints and rules based on customer sites. Its development combines photorealistic simulated scenarios with real-world safety testing. Humble says the system requires no mapping or predetermined route programming and that fine-tuning it for a specialized logistics environment takes no more than a few days.
Before making a move, the autonomy model produces a plain-language explanation of what it sees, what it is deciding and why. Humble says this reasoning directly shapes the vehicle’s action and makes each decision traceable and auditable.
